summary:
Amasya stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and the record contains no Amasya-specific provision, ordinance or enforcement finding. What a trans visitor faces in Amasya is the country-wide regime described below, applied without documented local mitigation or local aggravation.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus '11th Judicial Package', reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people. Human Rights Watch described it as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison; participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would carry up to four years, and since same-sex marriage is not legal in Türkiye, such ceremonies are by definition symbolic.

The same package would restrict gender-affirming care: the surgery age raised from 18 to 25, permanent infertility made mandatory, with medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years and transgender patients facing up to three years for care outside the new limits. Human Rights Watch states this would force treatment into underground settings.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records six right-to-life violations, three of them logged as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these counts are drawn from media and civil-society reports.

The same report documents 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, alongside 336 assembly violations and 313 liberty violations. The liberty figure represents a roughly 2.5-fold rise, consisting mostly of detentions, with event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings.

Hostility is institutionalised through 'Year of the Family' instructions to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. These measures operate as country-wide practice rather than provincial choice, and no Amasya-specific finding appears in the report.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern documented by Kaos GL and Human Rights Watch is uniform across Türkiye's provinces; Amasya offers no evidence of either a more permissive local practice or a harsher one. A visitor should expect the same checkpoint, document and assembly risks in Amasya as in Istanbul or Ankara.

The pending status of the 11th Judicial Package does not signal restraint. Reporting from Istanbul in 2025 shows police applying GBT ('General Information Gathering') stops to trans women before the package was enacted, with detainees noting that enforcement preceded the law. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match passport gender marker.

Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every document check is therefore an occasion on which presentation can be compared against passport data.
localsOnly:
Residents of Amasya live under the same national framework as visitors, with no provincial carve-out. The 11th Judicial Package, if enacted, would set the penalties described above for conduct deemed contrary to 'biological sex and general morality' and would tighten the conditions under which gender-affirming care can be provided, including the raised surgery age and infertility requirement.

Trans people in Türkiye are placed in prisons according to registered sex; a trans man has been held in a women's prison, and custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation in parliament by the end of 2025. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer, binary and heteronormative administration, and ineffective complaints mechanisms.

A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option on medical-board reports and required e-reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
outOfScopeNotes:
The record contains no Amasya-specific finding on any dimension of this assessment: no local ordinance, no local enforcement pattern, no local violence incident, no local facility or care access data. The province-level layer is unresolved rather than cleared, and the absence of a local record should not be read as evidence of local tolerance.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted as of the visitor's travel date is not sourced here; the inventory records it as a leaked draft reported on 29 October 2025. Visitors should verify current status before travel.

The Kaos GL counts rest on media and civil-society reporting because Türkiye maintains no official hate-crime statistics; the true totals may be higher. This limitation is stated by the source and is not resolved in this record.
